facts.claim: 'The Highway Song (OurVinyl Sessions)' by Kat Hasty and OurVinyl was released as a single on November 18, 2021. It runs about 3 minutes and is copyrighted to OurVinyl.

The OurVinyl Sessions version of the song is track 3 on the 4-song collection 'Kat Hasty | OurVinyl Sessions', released January 4, 2022. The other tracks are 'Where the Wildflowers Lay', 'Bleed For You' and 'The Devil In Us All'.
Bandcamp credits the session track to Kathryn Camille Hasty and OurVinyl. Its tags include alternative americana, country folk, singer-songwriter and unplugged.
Kathryn Camille Hasty is listed as the writer and composer of 'The Highway Song'. The studio version appears on her album 'Drowning In Dreams'.

Hasty said 'The Highway Song' is probably her favorite of her songs. She wrote it after she started singing a line while driving to Fort Worth. By the time she stopped for gas and food, she had written the whole song in her head, and she then typed it up on her phone.
Hasty has said 'The Highway Song' is the one she screams in the car.
Kat Hasty is a country singer-songwriter and a native of West Texas. She self-released her debut EP 'Drowning In Dreams Vol. 1' in 2020.
Her 2020 single 'Pretty Things', from the EP 'Drowning In Dreams Vol. 2', became a breakthrough hit after going viral on social media.

Hasty grew up on rock 'n' roll through her father and later leaned toward folk rock such as Bob Dylan. Her sound has been described as mixing a Bob Dylan sound, Miranda Lambert inspiration and the West Texas lifestyle.

Her bio says she was born and raised in West Texas, and her songwriting draws on desert highways and oil-town life. It also says she has released three EPs, a live session collection with OurVinyl, and two singles as of 2023.

research.lineage: The song sits in the West Texas country and folk-rock singer-songwriter tradition, with Bob Dylan and Miranda Lambert named as influences, in a stripped-back live-session format.

draft:
Halfway through **The Highway Song**, Kat Hasty lists the ways an old love keeps coming back: a sleepless night, a cocaine habit, and finally the thing you're listening to. "It comes in the form of a heartache song," the narrator admits, and the song quietly confesses that it is its own symptom. That's a sly bit of writing, and it's what this OurVinyl session version makes plain. With nothing around the words, the admission has nowhere to hide.

The story starts at 17, with a man who didn't love the narrator back. Everything after is an attempt to fill the space he left, mostly by breaking other people's hearts. The chorus is where the self-justification lives. There's a nameless highway, Mary Jane, one bummed cigarette that turned into chain-smoking, and a man from Oklahoma who got told he was loved. Then the shrug: "But I was born for leaving." It sounds like fate, but the verses have already shown it's a wound wearing fate's clothes. The cigarette detail does the same work in miniature. One casual borrow becomes a habit, and that's how the leaving started too.

The second verse is the most tender stretch. Tired and alone, the narrator looks at the first man's pictures and decides "He's better off on his own." Pride, grief, and a kind of generosity all sit in that line, and none of them wins. He is still "everything that I have ever known," which is a devastating thing to say about someone who never loved you back.

Hasty wrote it in one sitting on the road to Fort Worth. She started singing a line while driving and had the whole song in her head by the time she stopped for gas and food, then typed it into her phone. She's called it probably her favorite of her songs, and the one she screams in the car. Here it isn't screamed. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar walks a steady bass line at a slow, flowing pace. Hasty's voice is clear and a little breathy, with no harmonies and no reverb to soften it, and the room sounds small and close. The delivery is direct, almost plain, which suits a narrator too worn out to dramatize.

It's West Texas songwriting with the Dylan habit of letting a list carry the feeling, and some of Miranda Lambert's unrepentant wildness in the chorus. The song ends on its last line, repeated, "I'll be gone in the morning," and by then it no longer sounds like a boast.

The song sticks because it lets you hear someone call running away a destiny while every other line shows it's still the same heartbreak from 17.
